title: Normal male karyotype
clinical_history: A 32-year-old man is studied as a control specimen during cytogenetics laboratory instruction. No congenital anomalies or hematologic disease are described.
unknown_prompt: Arrange the chromosomes from this demonstration metaphase into a standard karyotype and report the ISCN.
plain_language_interpretation: A normal male diploid karyotype: 46 chromosomes with one X and one Y chromosome and no numerical or structural abnormality reported.
diagnosis: No cytogenetic abnormality identified (normal male karyotype)
diagnosis_options: No cytogenetic abnormality identified (normal male karyotype)
No cytogenetic abnormality identified (normal female karyotype)
explanation: A standard male karyotype contains 22 pairs of autosomes plus X and Y. Chromosomes are arranged by the Denver/ISCN groups using relative length and centromere position: A (1–3), B (4–5), C (6–12 and X), D (13–15), E (16–18), F (19–20), and G (21–22 and Y). The ISCN 46,XY states the chromosome number first, then the sex-chromosome complement, with no additional abnormality tokens.
hints: Count the chromosomes in the unassigned tray before you begin grouping. A normal human metaphase has 46 chromosomes.
Place the two largest metacentric chromosomes in group A as pair 1. Pair 2 is large and more submetacentric; pair 3 is slightly smaller and nearly metacentric.
The Y chromosome is a small acrocentric chromosome with a dark-staining q arm; it belongs in group G with 21 and 22, not with the C-group X chromosome.
